title: If and then
verifiedBy: Claude Opus 5 — LLM review, authorised by repo owner

rules.text: yadi opens the condition and tarhi opens the consequence, and each of them sits at the FRONT of its own clause — exactly where English puts 'if' and 'then'. That makes the placement the easy half of this module; everything difficult about it is in the verb.

tarhi CAN BE DROPPED. yadi bhavatī icchati bhavatī idam pustakam paṭhet is a complete, ordinary sentence with no tarhi in it. This is the sharp contrast with L3-M2: that module's saḥ or tat may never be left out, and this module's tarhi may. Two pairs, opposite rules.

The optative opens here. It is the mood of should, could and might, and this course writes exactly ONE cell of it: the third singular, formed with -et — gacchet, paṭhet, khādet. bhavān gṛham gacchet is 'you should go home'. It advises; it does not order.

The -et cell is the one bhavān and bhavatī already take, so advice lands in the register this course has spoken since L1-M2: the person in front of you, with a third-person verb. Opening one cell cost no second decision, which is exactly why this one was chosen.

What does NOT come with it, so you know the shape of the hole: the first-person optative gaccheyam, every dual and plural shape, and kuryāt — the optative of L1-M4's karoti, which does not end in -et at all and belongs to another pattern. None of them is written anywhere in this course.

A condition does not require the optative. yadi bhavān adya na gacchati tarhi śvaḥ gacchatu is a plain present in the first half and L2-M4's polite imperative in the second, and it is completely ordinary. The two systems meet here; they are not the same system.

Prohibition is na plus the optative: bhavān adya na gacchet, 'you shouldn't go today'. Sanskrit has a second negative word for telling someone not to do something, and it comes with a set of verb forms this course has not opened, so it is written nowhere here.

English has a past counterfactual — 'if I had gone, I would have seen it' — and there is no way to build it from what you have. It needs forms this course has not opened. Every condition in this module is about now or about what happens next.

L2-M1's kṛpayā stacks straight on top of advice when the advice is pressed: kṛpayā bhavān gṛham gacchet. Nothing about the verb changes; the please is a separate word and it goes first, as it always has.

A wish takes the same frame as advice and there is no separate wish form to learn. What you want for somebody and what you advise them to do come out of this one ending, and the difference lives in the situation rather than in the grammar.

sentences.display: yadi bhavān adya gacchati tarhi aham api gacchāmi.
sentences.script: यदि भवान् अद्य गच्छति तर्हि अहम् अपि गच्छामि।
sentences.cue: If you go today, then I will go too.
sentences.literal: if you today go then I also go

words.note: 'If'. It takes no ending and it opens its clause, where English puts it. The clause it opens is complete on its own and comes first.
L1-M2's 'you' for a man, with a third-person verb — the register this course has spoken from its second module.
L1-M4's 'today'.
L1-M2's 'goes', the plain present. A condition does not need a special verb form; this one is as ordinary as it looks.
'Then'. It opens the consequence, it takes no ending, and unlike L3-M2's correlative it may be left out without breaking the sentence.
L1-M1's 'I'. The consequence has its own subject, because it is about a different person from the condition.
L1-M10's 'also'. It sits AFTER the word it attaches to, so aham api is 'I too' — the placement law that ca and api share.
L1-M2's 'I go'. Both halves are in the plain present, which is what makes this the simplest shape a condition takes.

sentences.trap: There is no future tense anywhere in this sentence and it still means the future. A condition about what happens next is built out of two plain presents; the simple future gamiṣyāmi is available and is not needed.
sentences.sound: YA-di bha-VAAN A-dya GACH-cha-ti TAR-hi a-HAM A-pi GACH-chhaa-mi. tarhi has the r and h running together, one join, no vowel between.

variations.display: yadi bhavān adya gacchati aham api gacchāmi.
variations.script: यदि भवान् अद्य गच्छति अहम् अपि गच्छामि।
variations.cue: If you go today, I will go too.
variations.changed: tarhi dropped and nothing else touched — the sentence is still complete, which is the one thing L3-M2's pair could never do

variations.display: yadi bhavatī adya gacchati tarhi aham api gacchāmi.
variations.script: यदि भवती अद्य गच्छति तर्हि अहम् अपि गच्छामि।
variations.cue: If you go today, then I will go too. (speaking to a woman)
variations.changed: the person addressed becomes a woman; the verb does not move, because a third-person verb says nothing about gender

variations.display: yadi bhavān adya na gacchati tarhi aham api na gacchāmi.
variations.script: यदि भवान् अद्य न गच्छति तर्हि अहम् अपि न गच्छामि।
variations.cue: If you do not go today, then I will not go either.
variations.changed: both halves negated separately, each on its own verb — the condition and the consequence do not share a na

sentences.usage: The plainest kind of bargain: what I do depends on what you do. Nothing in it is advice and nothing in it is a wish, which is why it needs no new verb form at all.
sentences.mnemonic: yadi in front of the if, tarhi in front of the then, and the verbs stay where they were.

words.note: L1-M2's 'you' for a man. The optative shape this module opens is the third-person one, which is exactly the one bhavān has always taken.
L1-M6's house, as a destination.
The optative of L1-M2's gacchati: the stem with -et on the end. It is advice, not an order, and it is the only cell of this mood the course writes. A row of its own here, pointing back at gacchati.

sentences.trap: gacchet is not a polite gacchatu. gacchatu tells someone to go; gacchet says that going would be the better thing. One is an instruction handed over, the other is a view offered.
sentences.sound: bha-VAAN GRI-ham GACH-chhet. The -et is one short syllable and the final t is unreleased, closed off with the tongue.

variations.display: bhavatī gṛham gacchet.
variations.script: भवती गृहम् गच्छेत्।
variations.cue: You should go home. (speaking to a woman)
variations.changed: the person addressed becomes a woman and the verb is untouched — one cell of the optative serves both

variations.display: bhavān gṛham na gacchet.
variations.script: भवान् गृहम् न गच्छेत्।
variations.cue: You shouldn't go home.
variations.changed: na in front of the optative, which is the whole of prohibition in this course — no second negative word is needed or written

variations.display: bhavān gṛham gacchatu.
variations.script: भवान् गृहम् गच्छतु।
variations.cue: Please go home.
variations.changed: the advice becomes L2-M4's polite imperative; the two forms sit one letter apart and do quite different work

mistake.why: gacchema is the 'let us' shape of this same mood, and a grammar book will have offered it. L2-M6 named it and refused to write it, and that refusal stands: this course opens the third singular -et and nothing else, so a plan for a group is still the plain present gacchāmaḥ.

sentences.usage: Advice to the person in front of you. It is the most ordinary thing this module can say and it carries no weight of authority — that is exactly why the third-person register suits it.
sentences.mnemonic: One cell only: -et, and only for the person you are talking to.

sentences.display: yadi bhavān khinnaḥ tarhi bhavān gṛham gacchet.
sentences.script: यदि भवान् खिन्नः तर्हि भवान् गृहम् गच्छेत्।
sentences.cue: If you are unhappy, then you should go home.
sentences.literal: if you unhappy then you home should-go

words.note: 'If', opening the condition. The condition here has no verb at all — a verbless nominal clause is as good a condition as any other.
L1-M2's 'you' for a man, subject of the condition.
L1-M9's 'unhappy', masculine to agree with bhavān. A woman addressed would be khinnā, and bhavatī with her.
'Then', at the front of the consequence. Dropping it here would be perfectly good Sanskrit; keeping it makes the two halves easier to hear apart.
The same 'you' again. Each clause carries its own subject, and Sanskrit does not mind repeating it across the join.
L1-M6's house, as a destination.
The optative of L1-M2's gacchati. Advice, in the one cell this course opens, sitting where the condition's consequence belongs.

sentences.trap: The condition has no verb and needs none, but the consequence does need its -et. A condition can be a bare adjective; advice cannot be.

variations.display: yadi bhavatī khinnā tarhi bhavatī gṛham gacchet.
variations.script: यदि भवती खिन्ना तर्हि भवती गृहम् गच्छेत्।
variations.cue: If you are unhappy, then you should go home. (speaking to a woman)
variations.changed: both halves move to the feminine at once — the pronoun and the adjective, and the verb again does not move

variations.display: kṛpayā bhavān gṛham gacchet.
variations.script: कृपया भवान् गृहम् गच्छेत्।
variations.cue: Please, you should go home.
variations.changed: the condition dropped and L2-M1's please added in front; the advice is now pressed rather than offered

variations.display: yadi bhavān khinnaḥ tarhi bhavān gṛham gacchatu.
variations.script: यदि भवान् खिन्नः तर्हि भवान् गृहम् गच्छतु।
variations.cue: If you are unhappy, then go home.
variations.changed: the advice becomes an instruction, which is a different thing to say to someone who has just told you they are unhappy

sentences.usage: Advice with the reason for it stated as a condition. It is gentler than bare advice, because the condition hands the other person the decision about whether it applies.

sentences.display: yadi bhavān adya na gacchati tarhi śvaḥ gacchatu.
sentences.script: यदि भवान् अद्य न गच्छति तर्हि श्वः गच्छतु।
sentences.cue: If you are not going today, then go tomorrow.
sentences.literal: if you today not go then tomorrow let-go

words.note: 'If'. There is no optative anywhere in this sentence, and it is still a completely ordinary condition.
L1-M2's 'you'. The consequence does not repeat it, because the imperative already points at the same person.
L1-M4's 'today'.
L1-M2's 'not', in front of the verb of the condition. Negating the condition does nothing to the consequence.
L1-M2's plain present.
'Then', opening the consequence.
L1-M6's 'tomorrow'.
L2-M4's polite imperative, not the optative. It hands over an instruction, and a condition is perfectly happy to end in one.

sentences.trap: The conditional and the optative are two systems that meet here, not one system. This sentence has a condition and no optative in it; S02 has an optative and no condition. Neither needs the other.
sentences.sound: YA-di bha-VAAN A-dya na GACH-cha-ti TAR-hi SHVAH GACH-cha-tu. śvaḥ is one syllable, the sh and v run together at the front.

variations.display: yadi bhavān adya na gacchati tarhi śvaḥ gacchet.
variations.script: यदि भवान् अद्य न गच्छति तर्हि श्वः गच्छेत्।
variations.cue: If you are not going today, then you should go tomorrow.
variations.changed: the instruction becomes advice — one ending apart, and the whole force of the sentence changes with it

variations.display: yadi bhavān adya na gacchati śvaḥ gacchatu.
variations.script: यदि भवान् अद्य न गच्छति श्वः गच्छतु।
variations.cue: If you are not going today, go tomorrow.
variations.changed: tarhi dropped; the two clauses stand side by side and the sentence is unharmed

variations.display: yadi bhavatī adya na gacchati tarhi śvaḥ gacchatu.
variations.script: यदि भवती अद्य न गच्छति तर्हि श्वः गच्छतु।
variations.cue: If you are not going today, then go tomorrow. (speaking to a woman)
variations.changed: the person addressed becomes a woman; nothing in the sentence but the pronoun records it

mistake.display: yadi aham gatavān tarhi aham pustakam paṭhitavān.
mistake.why: An attempt at 'if I had gone, I would have read the book'. The participial past states a fact — 'I went' — so this reads as 'if I went, then I read the book', which is not what was meant. The past counterfactual needs forms this course has not opened and is written nowhere in it.

sentences.usage: Rearranging a plan when the first version has fallen through. The condition carries the bad news and the consequence carries the fix.

sentences.display: yadi bhavatī icchati bhavatī idam pustakam paṭhet.
sentences.script: यदि भवती इच्छति भवती इदम् पुस्तकम् पठेत्।
sentences.cue: If you like, you could read this book.
sentences.literal: if you want you this book should-read

words.note: 'If'. This sentence has no tarhi at all and is not missing anything — that is the rule this hero exists to show.
L1-M2's 'you' for a woman, with a third-person verb.
L1-M3's 'wants'. yadi bhavatī icchati is the softest opening this module has, because it hands the decision over before the advice arrives.
The same 'you' again, now the subject of the consequence.
L1-M1's 'this', neuter for pustakam.
L1-M1's book, as the thing being read.
The optative of L1-M4's paṭhati: the stem with -et. Its own row here, pointing back at paṭhati, because a level never edits a file below it.

sentences.trap: Nothing is missing from this sentence. An English speaker who has met L3-M2's obligatory correlative will hear the gap where tarhi would be and want to fill it. The two constructions look alike and the rule is the opposite.
sentences.sound: YA-di bha-va-TII ICH-cha-ti bha-va-TII I-dam PUS-ta-kam PA-thhet. The -ṭh- of paṭhet is one breathed sound made with the tongue curled back.

variations.display: yadi bhavatī icchati tarhi bhavatī idam pustakam paṭhet.
variations.script: यदि भवती इच्छति तर्हि भवती इदम् पुस्तकम् पठेत्।
variations.cue: If you like, then you could read this book.
variations.changed: tarhi put back in; the meaning does not change, which is the proof that it was optional in the first place

variations.display: yadi bhavān icchati bhavān idam pustakam paṭhet.
variations.script: यदि भवान् इच्छति भवान् इदम् पुस्तकम् पठेत्।
variations.cue: If you like, you could read this book. (speaking to a man)
variations.changed: both halves move to the masculine pronoun together; a mixed pair would be two different people

variations.display: yadi bhavatī na icchati bhavatī idam pustakam na paṭhet.
variations.script: यदि भवती न इच्छति भवती इदम् पुस्तकम् न पठेत्।
variations.cue: If you don't want to, you shouldn't read this book.
variations.changed: both halves negated — the second na sits in front of the optative, which is how this course says 'shouldn't'

mistake.why: This is L3-M2's correlative with its saḥ dropped, and it is broken — the main clause has no subject at all. Set it beside this module's hero, which has dropped its tarhi and is perfectly good. Two pairs that look alike, and only one of them can lose its second half.

sentences.usage: Offering a suggestion without pressing it. The condition yadi bhavatī icchati is the nearest this course comes to 'if you want', and it is what keeps advice from sounding like instruction.
sentences.mnemonic: tarhi may go; saḥ may not. That is the difference between the two pairs.

words.note: L1-M2's 'you' for a man.
L1-M4's 'today'.
L1-M2's 'not'. Put in front of an optative it becomes the whole of prohibition — there is no other word to learn for it here.
The optative of L1-M2's gacchati. na gacchet is 'shouldn't go', and the negation sits outside the verb rather than inside it.

sentences.trap: na plus the optative advises against something. It does not forbid it. Sanskrit does have a word that forbids, it comes with verb forms this course has not opened, and it is written nowhere here.

variations.display: bhavatī adya na gacchet.
variations.script: भवती अद्य न गच्छेत्।
variations.cue: You shouldn't go today. (speaking to a woman)
variations.changed: the person addressed becomes a woman; the verb and the negation are untouched

variations.display: bhavān adya gacchet.
variations.script: भवान् अद्य गच्छेत्।
variations.cue: You should go today.
variations.changed: na removed, and advice against becomes advice for — one word carries the whole reversal

variations.display: bhavān adya na paṭhet.
variations.script: भवान् अद्य न पठेत्।
variations.cue: You shouldn't read today.
variations.changed: a different verb in the same cell, which is the point: the ending is the lesson and it sits on any of these stems

mistake.why: The plain present has been used where advice was meant. As written this reports a fact — 'you are not going today' — rather than offering a view about it. The whole of the difference is the -et.

sentences.usage: Advising against something, which in this register is as gentle as advising for it. Nothing about it is a command, and nobody hears it as one.
sentences.mnemonic: na in front, -et on the end, and nothing else is needed to say shouldn't.

sentences.display: yadi mārgaḥ dīrghaḥ tarhi bhavān yānena gacchet.
sentences.script: यदि मार्गः दीर्घः तर्हि भवान् यानेन गच्छेत्।
sentences.cue: If the road is long, then you should go by vehicle.
sentences.literal: if road long then you by-vehicle should-go

words.note: 'If', opening a verbless condition about a thing rather than about the person being advised.
L2-M4's road. The condition's subject has nothing to do with the consequence's subject, and that is allowed.
L2-M2's 'long', masculine to agree with mārgaḥ.
'Then'. With two different subjects on either side, tarhi is worth keeping — it marks where one clause stops and the other starts.
L1-M2's 'you', subject of the advice.
L2-M4's vehicle in the by-means-of shape. The optative takes exactly the same company the present did.
The optative of L1-M2's gacchati, advising a way of travelling rather than a destination.

sentences.trap: The two clauses have different subjects and neither borrows from the other. This is not the absolutive of L3-M1, which required one shared subject; a condition and its consequence may be about entirely different things.
sentences.sound: YA-di MAAR-gah DIIR-ghah TAR-hi bha-VAAN YAA-ne-na GACH-chhet. yānena is three even syllables with the long aa at the front.

variations.display: yadi mārgaḥ hrasvaḥ tarhi bhavān mārgeṇa gacchet.
variations.script: यदि मार्गः ह्रस्वः तर्हि भवान् मार्गेण गच्छेत्।
variations.cue: If the road is short, then you should go by the road.
variations.changed: the condition flips to the opposite adjective and the advice flips with it; mārgaḥ turns up twice, in two different shapes

variations.display: yadi mārgaḥ dīrghaḥ bhavān yānena gacchet.
variations.script: यदि मार्गः दीर्घः भवान् यानेन गच्छेत्।
variations.cue: If the road is long, you should go by vehicle.
variations.changed: tarhi dropped even with two different subjects; it costs a little clarity and no grammar

variations.display: yadi mārgaḥ dīrghaḥ tarhi bhavān yānena gacchatu.
variations.script: यदि मार्गः दीर्घः तर्हि भवान् यानेन गच्छतु।
variations.cue: If the road is long, then go by vehicle.
variations.changed: advice becomes instruction; with a fact for a condition, the instruction reads as the more helpful of the two

sentences.usage: Practical advice about how to do something, given because of a fact rather than because of how somebody feels. This is the shape most directions take.

sentences.display: yadi samasyā asti tarhi bhavān mahyam vadatu.
sentences.script: यदि समस्या अस्ति तर्हि भवान् मह्यम् वदतु।
sentences.cue: If there is a problem, then please tell me.
sentences.literal: if problem is then you to-me please-say

words.note: 'If'. The condition here is about the world rather than about either person in the conversation.
L2-M8's 'problem'.
L1-M3's 'is'. samasyā asti is 'there is a problem', with no word for 'there' in it.
'Then', opening the consequence. It could be dropped here and the sentence would stand.
L1-M2's 'you'. The imperative already points at him, and naming him as well is the ordinary polite thing to do.
L1-M1's 'to me', the shape a person takes when something is given or said to them.
L2-M7's polite imperative of 'says'. A request, not advice — this sentence opens no optative at all.

sentences.trap: Neither half of this sentence uses the mood the module opened. A condition is a joining word and a consequence can be anything: a statement, an instruction, a request, or advice.

variations.display: yadi samasyā asti tarhi kṛpayā bhavān mahyam vadatu.
variations.script: यदि समस्या अस्ति तर्हि कृपया भवान् मह्यम् वदतु।
variations.cue: If there is a problem, then please do tell me.
variations.changed: L2-M1's kṛpayā added in front of the consequence, pressing a request that was already polite

variations.display: yadi bhavataḥ samasyā asti tarhi bhavān mahyam vadatu.
variations.script: यदि भवतः समस्या अस्ति तर्हि भवान् मह्यम् वदतु।
variations.cue: If you have a problem, then please tell me.
variations.changed: the problem is given an owner with L1-M2's bhavataḥ, so the condition stops being about the world and becomes about him

variations.display: yadi samasyā asti bhavān mahyam vadatu.
variations.script: यदि समस्या अस्ति भवान् मह्यम् वदतु।
variations.cue: If there is a problem, tell me.
variations.changed: tarhi dropped; a short sentence loses nothing by it

mistake.display: yadi samasyā asti bhavān mahyam vadatu tarhi.
mistake.why: tarhi has been sent to the end. It may be left out of a sentence entirely, and it may not be moved: like yadi, it opens its own clause. Dropping a word and relocating it are not the same freedom.

sentences.usage: The standard offer of help. The condition keeps it from presuming that anything is wrong, which is why it is worth saying this way rather than simply asking.

sentences.display: yadi bhavān asvasthaḥ tarhi bhavān alpam khādet.
sentences.script: यदि भवान् अस्वस्थः तर्हि भवान् अल्पम् खादेत्।
sentences.cue: If you are unwell, then you should eat a little.
sentences.literal: if you unwell then you a-little should-eat

words.note: 'If', opening a verbless condition about how the person feels.
L1-M2's 'you' for a man.
L2-M8's 'unwell', masculine to agree with bhavān. A woman addressed is asvasthā.
'Then', opening the consequence.
The same 'you', now the subject of the advice.
L2-M9's 'a little', as the quantity eaten.
The optative of L1-M4's khādati: the stem with -et. Its own row here, pointing back at khādati, with no edit to L1-M4.

sentences.trap: khādet is the third -et in this module and the last one it writes. Three verbs are enough to show an ending; a fourth would teach nothing the rule has not already said.
sentences.sound: YA-di bha-VAAN as-VAS-thah TAR-hi bha-VAAN AL-pam KHAA-det. khādet starts with k plus breath, then a long aa.

variations.display: yadi bhavatī asvasthā tarhi bhavatī alpam khādet.
variations.script: यदि भवती अस्वस्था तर्हि भवती अल्पम् खादेत्।
variations.cue: If you are unwell, then you should eat a little. (speaking to a woman)
variations.changed: both halves to the feminine at once, pronoun and adjective together, and the verb unchanged

variations.display: yadi bhavān asvasthaḥ tarhi bhavān na khādet.
variations.script: यदि भवान् अस्वस्थः तर्हि भवान् न खादेत्।
variations.cue: If you are unwell, then you shouldn't eat.
variations.changed: the advice negated, and the quantity word drops out with it — na khādet advises against the whole thing

variations.display: yadi bhavān asvasthaḥ tarhi bhavān adhikam jalam pibatu.
variations.script: यदि भवान् अस्वस्थः तर्हि भवान् अधिकम् जलम् पिबतु।
variations.cue: If you are unwell, then drink more water.
variations.changed: the consequence becomes an instruction with a different verb — an optative was never required, only chosen

sentences.usage: Everyday advice to somebody who is not well. This module offers advice and nothing more: what to actually do about being ill belongs to L3-M7, which has the words for it.

sentences.display: yadi bhavatī adya na gacchati tarhi aham śvaḥ gacchāmi.
sentences.script: यदि भवती अद्य न गच्छति तर्हि अहम् श्वः गच्छामि।
sentences.cue: If you are not going today, then I will go tomorrow.
sentences.literal: if you today not go then I tomorrow go

words.note: 'If'. A condition and a plan: the longest ordinary shape this module builds.
L1-M2's 'you' for a woman, with a third-person verb.
L1-M4's 'today'.
L1-M2's 'not', in front of the condition's verb.
L1-M2's plain present.
'Then', opening the plan.
L1-M1's 'I'. The two halves are about two different people, so both subjects are written.
L1-M6's 'tomorrow'.
L1-M2's 'I go'. The plain present carries a plan about tomorrow without any help from the future, because śvaḥ has already said when.

sentences.trap: This is a wish and a plan at once, and neither of them has a form of its own. The wish lives in the situation; the grammar is two ordinary presents joined by yadi and tarhi.

variations.display: yadi bhavatī adya gacchati tarhi aham api adya gacchāmi.
variations.script: यदि भवती अद्य गच्छति तर्हि अहम् अपि अद्य गच्छामि।
variations.cue: If you are going today, then I will go today too.
variations.changed: the condition turned positive and the plan follows it back to today, with api marking that I am joining rather than replacing

variations.display: yadi bhavatī adya na gacchati aham śvaḥ gacchāmi.
variations.script: यदि भवती अद्य न गच्छति अहम् श्वः गच्छामि।
variations.cue: If you are not going today, I will go tomorrow.
variations.changed: tarhi dropped from the longest sentence in the module, which is where it is most useful and still not required

variations.display: yadi bhavatī adya na gacchati tarhi aham śvaḥ gamiṣyāmi.
variations.script: यदि भवती अद्य न गच्छति तर्हि अहम् श्वः गमिष्यामि।
variations.cue: If you are not going today, then I shall go tomorrow.
variations.changed: the plan takes L1-M2's simple future instead of the present — available, a little more definite, and never required

sentences.usage: Working out between two people who does what and when. Conditions do most of their everyday work here rather than in advice.
sentences.mnemonic: Two plain presents and two little words. Most conditions need nothing else.

comprehensionPool.display: yadi bhavān adya na khādati tarhi bhavān phalam khādet.
comprehensionPool.script: यदि भवान् अद्य न खादति तर्हि भवान् फलम् खादेत्।
comprehensionPool.cue: If you are not eating today, then you should eat some fruit.

comprehensionPool.display: yadi mārgaḥ dīrghaḥ tarhi aham yānena gacchāmi.
comprehensionPool.script: यदि मार्गः दीर्घः तर्हि अहम् यानेन गच्छामि।
comprehensionPool.cue: If the road is long, then I go by vehicle.

comprehensionPool.display: yadi samasyā asti tarhi aham sāhāyyam karomi.
comprehensionPool.script: यदि समस्या अस्ति तर्हि अहम् साहाय्यम् करोमि।
comprehensionPool.cue: If there is a problem, then I will help.
You shouldn't go to school today.

comprehensionPool.display: yadi bhavatī khinnā tarhi bhavatī mahyam vadatu.
comprehensionPool.script: यदि भवती खिन्ना तर्हि भवती मह्यम् वदतु।
comprehensionPool.cue: If you are unhappy, then please tell me.

comprehensionPool.display: yadi bhojanam uttamam tarhi aham adhikam khādāmi.
comprehensionPool.script: यदि भोजनम् उत्तमम् तर्हि अहम् अधिकम् खादामि।
comprehensionPool.cue: If the food is good, then I eat more.

comprehensionPool.display: yadi saḥ asvasthaḥ tarhi saḥ adya na gacchet.
comprehensionPool.script: यदि सः अस्वस्थः तर्हि सः अद्य न गच्छेत्।
comprehensionPool.cue: If he is unwell, then he shouldn't go today.

comprehensionPool.display: yadi bhavān icchati bhavān saṃskṛtam paṭhet.
comprehensionPool.script: यदि भवान् इच्छति भवान् संस्कृतम् पठेत्।
comprehensionPool.cue: If you like, you could study Sanskrit.

comprehensionPool.display: yadi adya bhojanam na asti tarhi aham phalam khādāmi.
comprehensionPool.script: यदि अद्य भोजनम् न अस्ति तर्हि अहम् फलम् खादामि।
comprehensionPool.cue: If there is no meal today, then I eat fruit.
Perhaps you should eat a little today.

comprehensionPool.display: yadi bhavatī saṃskṛtam jānāti tarhi bhavatī idam pustakam paṭhet.
comprehensionPool.script: यदि भवती संस्कृतम् जानाति तर्हि भवती इदम् पुस्तकम् पठेत्।
comprehensionPool.cue: If you know Sanskrit, then you should read this book.
True — you should go home today.
